title: Warrants used to search Andrew's homes were unlawful, court says
description: Thames Valley Police has accepted warrants it used to search Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor's homes at the time of his arrest in February were unlawful, t
body: Thames Valley Police has accepted warrants it used to search Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor's homes at the time of his arrest in February were unlawful, the High Court has been told.Following Thursday's hearing, items seized in the raid continue to be held by the police, with a further hearing to take place in 2027 to decide whether the material can be used as evidence. Meanwhile, the criminal investigation into Mountbatten-Windsor is ongoing.The former prince, who denies any wrongdoing, was arrested by police on 19 February on suspicion of misconduct in public office, after which he launched a legal challenge over the legality of the search warrants.The force said it accepted that the "initial court's decision to issue warrants under the specific piece of legislation used was incorrect" before they searched the properties.On Thursday at the High Court, judge Mr Justice Hilliard said Mountbatten-Windsor and the police had agreed that the search warrants had been unlawful.However, he added: "The fact that the search warrants were quashed does not bring the investigation to an end or mean that the whole of the investigation is unlawful."Mountbatten-Windsor opposes the police's bid to retain the evidence, the judge said, and another hearing is expected in 2027.The next stage in this legal dispute will be a behind-closed-doors hearing over whether the police can still retain material seized from Mountbatten-Windsor's homes under alternative powers designed for situations like this.The error that has led to Thames Valley Police accepting the search warrants were unlawful relates to the particular power the judge permitted the force to use when its officers raided the properties.Strict legal safeguards on searches bar the police from automatically seizing sensitive material without thinking through in advance the need to take it.Examples of that material include advice from a suspect's lawyer or material which does not really belong to them, such as copies of confidential work-related papers from an employer.In practice, if the police find such material during a search, they should return it rather than use it in their investigation.The category of search warrant that was granted by the court in this instance did not take into account the possibility of such protected material being seized.However, the law says police can in fact seize that kind of material - or potentially retain it in the event of an error - providing they pass some extra tests.Thames Valley Police must now convince a judge that the material is likely to be of "substantial value" to their investigation into Mountbatten-Windsor and, ultimately, potential evidence to present to a court. So while the force has conceded the search warrant was unlawful, a judge will have to decide whether this alternative search power, with its extra safeguards, justifies them keeping and using the material after all.

schema.headline: Warrants used to search Andrew's homes were unlawful, court says

title: Zack Polanski failed to show leadership over Zionism motion, ex-Green leader says
description: Zack Polanski failed to show leadership over a motion passed by Green Party members declaring Zionism a form of racism, the party's former leader Caro
body: Zack Polanski failed to show leadership over a motion passed by Green Party members declaring Zionism a form of racism, the party's former leader Caroline Lucas has told the BBC.Lucas told Newsnight that the party's current leader, who did not attend the debate on the motion at the Green Party's annual conference in Brighton, "should have been there and he should have voted".She described the motion, which defined Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state", as "dangerous" and "divisive".In the wake of the vote, Polanski has said he will not accept anyone being excluded from the Green Party "because of the religious or communal body they are part of".Lucas's comments came shortly after polls closed in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, where Polanski stood as a candidate, but before the result was declared.Polanski came second to Labour in the by-election, although Labour's majority was slashed from 11,572 to 3,364.Speaking after the result was declared, Polanski said he would continue as leader, adding: "Yes I've taken a loss tonight but our movement is so much bigger than one election or one motion."Asked whether he agreed with the decision by party members to vote that Zionism is racism, Polanski, who is Jewish, told reporters: "I grew up in a Zionist household and I grew up with the idea that that region was a land without a people and a people without a land and as I've educated myself, learned, discovered, I don't believe that's true. "And what we're seeing is an ongoing genocide and the displacement of the Palestinian people. I believe that's clearly racist."Israel has repeatedly denied its actions in Gaza amount to genocide.The International Court of Justice (ICJ) is currently hearing a case brought by South Africa that accuses Israeli forces of genocide, but it could take years to reach a conclusion. Israel has called the case "wholly unfounded" and based on "biased and false claims".Pressed again over whether he agreed that "Zionism is racism", he said: "The displacement of the Palestinian people, the genocide, is totally racist."Asked if he would apologise to Jewish people upset by the vote on the motion, Polanski said: "It's my job to reassure people and to make sure that we bring our party together. "Nobody will be excluded in the Green Party based on faith and religion."Polanski had declined media interviews in the final days of the by-election campaign, as his party faced criticism over the motion.His comments after the result were the first time he had answered questions on the issue since the motion passed.Polanski did not vote on the motion on Sunday after leaving the party's conference early to campaign in the north London constituency.The motion also backed a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.Under Green Party rules, motions supported by members become official party policy, but will not necessarily be included in the party's manifesto at the next general election.Lucas, who voted against the motion, said: "I would have hoped [Polanski] would have been a very strong critic of this motion."She added that it was "flawed from top to bottom".Asked if Polanski should stand down, she told Newsnight: "I think let's just see what happens in the coming days and weeks. Obviously he has been completely taken up with this by-election."I want him to speak now about what's happened, I want him to show the leadership that was frankly missing on Sunday. "I think the jury is out about whether he will do that - but I very much hope he will."In response to Lucas's comments, a Green Party source said: "There are ups and downs in politics and when people are passionate they disagree in the heat of a campaign. "We do things differently - unlike Labour who use anonymous sources and resort to  factionalism."The motion has overshadowed the final days of Polanski's by-election campaign, where the Greens had been hoping to overturn a substantial Labour majority in the seat vacated by former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer.It has sparked days of controversy and exposed divisions between the party's newly enlarged membership base under Polanski and its MPs elected at the last general election.Four of the five Green MPs opposed the motion, while the party's co-deputy leaders were split over whether they supported it.The vote also led to the resignation of the Green deputy leader in Wales and condemnation from the European Green Party.In a written statement on Monday, Polanski did not specify whether he supported the motion passed by members but sought to reassure Jewish members that "no-one will be made unwelcome because of their background, their faith, or where they worship".Polanski added that "antisemitism and criticism of the Israeli state are, and must always be, completely distinct".Ahead of the vote, he had backed an amendment to specify that the motion should not be used to discipline Jewish members attending synagogues that consider themselves Zionist, but this was voted down by members.He had also said he wanted to see the reference to a single Palestinian state changed, arguing: "I don't believe we as a Green Party of England and Wales, or even the British government, should be deciding what the future settlement looks like."Meanwhile, Prime Minister Andy Burnham has called on Polanski to reverse the motion and ensure it is not Green Party policy.In his first comment on the row, Burnham said it was "completely wrong" for the party to support the motion and this showed "terrible judgement".The PM said he felt the motion effectively ruled out a two-state solution between Israel and Palestine."For that reason, it shouldn't be supported in any way, shape or form," he told reporters while on a visit to Berlin.When asked if he would rule out entering into coalition with the Greens, he would not be drawn on "any business about what might or might not happen in the future".

schema.headline: Zack Polanski failed to show leadership over Zionism motion, ex-Green leader says

title: 'Add me to WhatsApp' scam calls to be investigated
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByTom MoseleyYou and YoursThe UK's data watchdog is investigating a spike in complaints about "robo calls" - where a recorde
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByTom MoseleyYou and YoursThe UK's data watchdog is investigating a spike in complaints about "robo calls" - where a recorded voice asks you to add them on WhatsApp - that are suspected to lead to a recruitment scam.The Information Commission's Office (ICO) had more than 3,600 complaints about automated calls in September - a five-year high and nearly three times the number it had in July.But it suspects millions of people are getting these calls and told BBC Radio 4's You and Yours it was "deeply concerned" by the sharp rise.The ICO advises people to ignore calls from numbers they don't recognise, and to block and report any suspicious calls to the watchdog.The automated calls typically come from what appears to be a UK mobile number.Some of the recorded messages mention an offer of part-time work.Simon Fell, from the Communications Crime Strategy Group, a telecoms industry body set up to tackle fraud, said he couldn't be sure exactly what form the scam would take as he hadn't followed up on the messages."Mostly likely it would be a recruitment scam," he said.Image caption, You and Yours added one of these numbers on WhatsApp and received this message"They would either put you through to a fake job listing, which might involve some form of money muling. It could look like a completely legitimate job, or something ad hoc, but they might pass criminal funds through your account which can lead to terrible consequences."It could also be a simple phishing exercise - criminals send out these messages, and what they really want to know is who's picking up, who's active - that information can be resold on the dark web."The possibilities are endless. At the end of the day this is a criminal that has reached out to you and they're trying to defraud you in some way shape or form."'Tip of the iceberg'Andy Curry, the ICO's head of criminal investigations, told the BBC he believed the calls were coming from abroad."We are trying to find who is behind this, why they're doing it and the impact it's having on members of the public," he said.The number of complaints received by the ICO would only be a small proportion of the totals affected, he said."We think there are probably millions of people who are receiving these messages, which appear to us to be largely indiscriminate."I've had them, my colleague who's leading the investigation has had them. It's likely to be tip of the iceberg."Fell said that mobile companies were "working on a range of fronts" to tackle the influx of automated calls.This includes sending intelligence reports to the regulator Ofcom, working with law enforcement, and liaising with Meta, which owns WhatsApp, because if someone does follow up on the request to add the number to the encrypted platform, "any dialogue that happens between you and the criminal then can't be investigated any further".A WhatsApp spokesman said there were features in place to protect its users from scam calls, including silencing calls from unknown numbers. He also said WhatsApp banned millions of accounts each year for "malicious behaviours", such as bulk account registration or automated messaging.Spoofed numbersWhile these calls typically appear to be from a UK mobile number, Fell said these numbers will be imitated, or spoofed, by the criminals behind the scam.Last November, the UK government promised, external that call spoofing would be eliminated within a year.A Home Office spokesman said the government was taking "robust action" to tackle scams."We remain committed to delivering the Telecommunications Charter, alongside industry, by November," he added.

schema.headline: 'Add me to WhatsApp' scam calls to be investigated

title: Olivia Colman on viral Wicker memes: 'This has never happened to me before'
description: Image source, Black Bear PicturesImage caption, Olivia Colman stars alongside Alexander Skarsgård in new film WickerByNoor NanjiCulture correspondent
body: Image source, Black Bear PicturesImage caption, Olivia Colman stars alongside Alexander Skarsgård in new film WickerByNoor NanjiCulture correspondent at London Film FestivalIt has already been described as 2026's weirdest rom-com, external.And new film Wicker has sparked a deluge of viral memes and steamy jokes that have flooded social media ahead of its release.Speaking to the BBC at its London Film Festival premiere, lead star Olivia Colman said she never expected such a big reaction."No, literally this has never happened for anything I've done before," she said."But you put Alexander Skarsgård in an interesting outfit, and everyone is looking."The film tells the tale of a lonely, ostracised fisherwoman (Colman) living in a medieval village. Tired of constantly being mocked for being single, she hires a basketmaker to mould her a new partner made entirely out of wicker.Enter Skarsgård - but not as you've ever seen him before.As the "wicker husband", he emerges as a strapping, dashing life-size piece of furniture.And he proves to be a devoted partner, and passionate lover, sparking jealousy among the other village women.Image source, Gareth Cattermole/Getty Images for BFIThe film has an A-list cast, with other stars including Peter Dinklage as the basket weaver, Elizabeth Debicki as the tailor's wife, and Richard E Grant as the village doctor.Since the release of the trailer, there's been a huge buzz online around the film - from BookTok and FilmTok fans swooning over Skarsgård’s character, to questions being asked over splinter risks during the film's erotic scenes.Swedish giant Ikea even got involved, posting photos of its rattan furniture on Instagram in a nod to the film, with the caption “husband material”.When asked why she thinks people are so fascinated and so thirsty for the wicker husband, Colman answered: "We all love a little bit of escapism. That's what film is beautiful for."And it's magical, and a bit of fantasy, and people love that, especially currently. What's not to love about a little bit of escapism and fantasy?"She also said it was the film's originality that drew her to it.Image source, Laura Rose/Dave Benett/WireImage"You get a lot of scripts through the post, and you feel like you've seen a bit before. And this, I really hadn't seen this before, so I was excited," she said.Like Colman, Debicki agrees that Skarsgård is the main reason the film has lit up the internet."I think it was a lot to do with Alex in a wicker man costume, really," she told the BBC. "I think that's something that apparently everybody would like to see."But Skarsgård himself gives all the credit to the designers of the outfit. "All I had to do was get stuck into it," he says.He also said the sex scenes were "super fun" to shoot."We wanted those moments when the bed crashes and breaks, and the way they comment on that in the scene is quite comedic," he said."But [the characters] also have tender moments and sexy moments, it was great."Image source, Black Bear PicturesImage caption, The steamy new rom-com has been causing a stir at film festivalsThe film is based on the short story The Wicker Husband by Ursula Wills-Jones. After its premiere at Sundance film festival earlier this year, The Guardian awarded it, external two stars, praising the "eye-catching premise" but cautioning that there was "too much wood but not enough fire".But The Hollywood Reporter, external was more positive, calling it "a warming, sometimes poignant pleasure".Away from the social media buzz, the film's stars say it also taps into deeper themes, from gender roles to breaking societal rules."It's very funny and strange and wonderful, but I find it very moving. And it's a good one to discover beyond the Ikea memes," said Debicki."It touches on a lot of stuff. Hierarchy, social structure," said Skarsgård. "But it's done with such a light touch.""It's about love, and it is funny, but it's also a romance, and it very gently laughs at the sort of traditions we have in marriage and community," said Colman."I think it's something that you will come out and discuss a lot."Wicker is released in UK cinemas on October 30.

schema.headline: Olivia Colman on viral Wicker memes: 'This has never happened to me before'

title: Russian strike on buses kills at least 30, say officials, as deadly attacks on Ukraine surge
description: At least 30 people have been killed in a Russian glide bomb attack on two civilian buses in the eastern front line city of Kramatorsk, rescue official
body: At least 30 people have been killed in a Russian glide bomb attack on two civilian buses in the eastern front line city of Kramatorsk, rescue officials say.Authorities said three people were also killed in the village of Bilenke, part of the Kramatorsk community.Another 18 people were wounded, said Donetsk regional head Vadym Filashkin, accusing Russia of targeting buses carrying passengers to kill as many civilians as possible.Kramatorsk and neighbouring Slovyansk are part of a so-called fortress belt that Moscow is trying to seize as part of Russian President Vladimir Putin's claim to the entire Ukrainian industrial region of Donbas.Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky said: "This strike will not go without our response."In a post on Telegram, he said: "Russia is trying to destroy all life in Donbas, and the world needs to react to this. React harshly - exactly as the Russians deserve for all the deaths they have caused."Images posted by local prosecutors showed the burning metal shell of the bus along with debris and some of the victims on the road.Moscow is yet to comment on the latest attack. It follows a dramatic surge in Russian attacks across Ukraine and a heavy increase in civilian casualties. According to the UN, Ukraine saw more civilians killed by August this year than were killed in all of 2025.In one single attack that destroyed a five-storey block of flats in Pryluky east of Kyiv early on Wednesday, 22 people were killed, including five children. Three of the children were only one year old.UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who together with Zelensky visited the site of the Russian strike in Pryluky, said the attack showed Putin's "evil intent and evil strategy".He announced "more sanctions on Russia, on the war machine of Putin, on the shadow fleet, on the oil companies, on the crypto, on the financing of the war" and told Zelensky the UK would stand with Ukraine "as long as it takes for you to prevail in this conflict".After the deadly attack on Kramatorsk, Filashkin appealed to anyone who was still in the eastern front line region to move to safer parts of Ukraine.Given the sharp deterioration of security in the two neighbouring cities, he said all public transport had been ordered to stop. The safety of civilians was paramount, and "we have no right to risk the lives of passengers and drivers", he said.Moscow has often cited the "liberation" and "protection" of the predominantly Russian-speaking Donbas as justification for the full-scale invasion of Ukraine launched by Putin in 2022 - a claim rejected by Ukraine and its allies as baseless.Donbas is made up of two regions - Luhansk and Donetsk - and with most of Luhansk under Russian control, the Kremlin is also aiming to capture remaining 20% of Donetsk territory still held by Ukraine.For much of the war Kramatorsk acted as a logistics and supply hub for the Ukrainian military, however it has now come under almost daily Russian attack as its military moves closer to the east of the city.Glide bombs in particular have been launched at Slovyansk and Kramatorsk. The bombs are fitted with winglets so they glide towards their target rather than simply fall.  In late August as many as nine glide bombs were fired at Kramatorsk in one day.Kramatorsk city council described the strike as a "horrific crime committed by the Russian army against the civilian population"."Once again, the Russians have struck a location where there are absolutely no military targets," it said. Russia has in recent weeks been launching constant air raids on the capital Kyiv, with sirens ringing virtually non-stop.On Thursday, Kyiv police said four people were killed and two injured in the latest Russian attack on the city.The attacks are forcing schoolchildren out of classes into underground shelters, shuttering businesses, and disrupting public transport. Moscow's strikes on Ukraine's key infrastructure, particularly on its energy grid, are causing power outages already and are even affecting the water supply. Local water authorities in the capital warned on Thursday that pressure was dropping across the city's right bank due to power cuts.Kyiv's metro network - which millions of residents rely on - on Thursday briefly halted all its train traffic due to a voltage drop from "external power centres". Trains later started moving again - but at greater intervals, local officials said.Zelensky offered his condolences to families and loved ones affected by the latest attack and said Ukraine's partners needed to provide "concrete action through new defence packages for the protection of Ukraine". Ahead of the Pryluky attack, the Ukrainian leader had warned this week of intelligence suggesting plans for a major Russian onslaught, and in Kyiv families responded by heading to metro stations for shelter.Such warnings are for now one of the only defences Ukrainians have.Interceptor missiles are in short supply around the world, so Ukraine has little  chance to stop incoming Russian ballistics. Both Russia and Ukraine have intensified long-range strikes on each other in recent months, with Russian attacks targeting Ukrainian data centres and logistics warehouses.On Thursday, Russian state-run media reported that a number of websites in the country were inaccessible following a Ukrainian drone attack on a data centre of Yandex - Russia's largest search engine.

schema.headline: Russian strike on buses kills at least 30, say officials, as deadly attacks on Ukraine surge

title: ADHD and autism at risk of over-diagnosis, says government review
description: The Watsons are just one family who have experience of this. Ryan and his wife knew there was something different with their son Atlas when he was aro
body: The Watsons are just one family who have experience of this. Ryan and his wife knew there was something different with their son Atlas when he was around 12 to 18 months old and missing development milestones.But it took three years to get an autism assessment. As time passed, his needs became increasingly clear. Now nearly seven, Atlas is non-verbal, still wears nappies and relies on others for all aspects of daily care.Despite this, Ryan said there was no fast-track route for children with the most complex needs. "You basically go on the list and wait however long until you get to the top."The wait left the family racing against time to secure support before Atlas started school. Ryan and his wife feared he would be placed in a mainstream school."We were terrified," Ryan says. "Anyone who has a child like Atlas will have the same panic that they'll start in a mainstream school where it's not safe."The strain was immense. "It was like I had two jobs," Ryan says. "I was going to work and then coming home and dealing with these things."Atlas was eventually diagnosed only months before starting school. The review said not every difficulty required a medical response and there was a risk of blurring the lines between diagnosable ADHD and autism and what should be considered the normal human variation in brain function, cognition and behaviour.It said there was a risk society was now moving from an era of under-diagnosis to over-diagnosis or mis-diagnosis, pointing to data showing more than 4% of children aged six to 17 were now diagnosed with autism, well above the 1-2% that studies suggest is the true level.But it said because some of these figures date back nearly a decade it was not possible to be absolutely certain or conclude over-diagnosis was currently occurring at scale.Mel Merritt, of the National Autistic Society, said the report shows that successive governments "have failed autistic people"."The harm and distress autistic people are facing is real and widespread and there is a desperate need to build a system that supports the needs of autistic people."Abigail Ampofo, of charity YoungMinds, said: "For years, young people have told us they feel blamed for their mental health or accused of making it up. We hope this review goes some way to show them their distress is not their fault and the systems around them are failing."But she said that would require major reform.The government welcomed the publication of the report and said it would be setting out a new model of providing support in its forthcoming mental health strategy, which is expected before the end of the year, and also promised to introduce tougher regulation of ADHD and autism assessments.Health Secretary Yvette Cooper added: "Professor Fonagy's review has shown the importance of early intervention to address mental health and neurodevelopmental conditions and the huge distress these can cause."

schema.headline: ADHD and autism at risk of over-diagnosis, says government review

title: South Africa vs Australia: Pat Cummins speaks to Usman Khawaja about autobiography
description: Pat Cummins has spoken to Usman Khawaja about his former team-mate's upcoming autobiography, but the Australia captain said he has no concerns about p
body: Pat Cummins has spoken to Usman Khawaja about his former team-mate's upcoming autobiography, but the Australia captain said he has no concerns about potential sandpapergate revelations.On Friday, Australia will begin their first Test series in South Africa since the ball-tampering scandal erupted in Cape Town in 2018.At the time, captain Steve Smith, vice-captain David Warner and batter Cameron Bancroft were banned for their part in the plot.Since then, the four Australia bowlers who played in that match, including Cummins, have denied they had any prior knowledge of the plan to cheat.The quartet, who released a joint statement about the episode in 2021, are once again set to be united in the first Test against South Africa in Durban.Khawaja played in all four Tests in 2018 and retired from international cricket in January. His autobiography will be released in November."Uz gave me a buzz a few weeks back that he is releasing a book," said Cummins. "He didn't go into too much detail, just basically gave me the heads-up that he is doing a book and, as always, no worries."Tell your story. It's fine. It's obviously a long time ago and all the investigations, everything was done back then and we answered every question a million times."It was dealt with then and all I can say is that as a group, we have moved on and we are very happy with the last eight to nine years how we have been as a group and evolved and obviously my focus is on captaining the cricket team."At the time of the ball-tampering controversy, Smith explained it was devised by the "leadership group" of the Australian team on the third day of the third Test in Cape Town. Bancroft was caught rubbing sandpaper on the ball the same day.While Smith, Warner and Bancroft – all batters – were punished, there was never an explanation of how bowlers Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon did not notice a change in the state of the ball.In a 2021 interview with the Guardian, Bancroft was asked if the bowlers knew and replied: "It's pretty probably self-explanatory."Days after Bancroft's interview was published, Cummins, Starc, Hazlewood and Lyon released their statement which said: "We feel compelled to put the key facts on the record again."We did not know a foreign substance was taken onto the field to alter the condition of the ball until we saw the images on the big screen at Newlands."And to those who, despite the absence of evidence, insist that 'we must have known' about the use of a foreign substance simply because we are bowlers, we say this: The umpires during that Test match, Nigel Llong and Richard Illingworth, both very respected and experienced umpires, inspected the ball after the images surfaced on the TV coverage and did not change it because there was no sign of damage."We respectfully request an end to the rumour-mongering and innuendo. It has gone on too long and it is time to move on."Earlier this week, left-arm seamer Starc referenced the scandal when he said: "What's left to come out after eight years?"And, speaking on Thursday, Cummins said the episode was "a long time ago"."It's nothing new," the 33-year-old told ABC. "We've spoken about it a little bit. If the crowd gets rowdy or whatever, if someone needs an extra helping hand, we're around."To be honest, it's so long ago and we, as a group, move on from things pretty quickly. It hasn't taken up too much of our time."The trip to South Africa is the first in a year of high-profile away series for Australia. After what appears to be a stern challenge against New Zealand in their home summer, Cummins' men then travel to India and defend the Ashes in England next year.With all-rounder Cameron Green ruled out because of injury, the tourists are likely to choose between Cooper Connolly and Nic Maddinson for a place in the middle order.On a Durban pitch expected to turn, South Africa have included two spinners – Keshav Maharaj and Simon Harmer - in their XI.

schema.headline: South Africa vs Australia: Pat Cummins speaks to Usman Khawaja about autobiography

title: Fort Hood attacker's execution by firing squad will be livestreamed, Pentagon says
description: The public will be able to watch the execution of a former US Army major by firing squad, US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has said.A Defense Departm
body: The public will be able to watch the execution of a former US Army major by firing squad, US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has said.A Defense Department official told the BBC the execution of Nidal Hasan, who shot dead 13 unarmed US soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009, would be livestreamed.It is believed it would be the first public execution in the US in almost a century. The decision to livestream it is "unprecedented in the modern era" and "on uncertain legal terrain," said John Mills, a lawyer who works with inmates sentenced to death. "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public," Hegseth said. "People need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things."The Pentagon had announced earlier this week that it would execute Hasan in the first military execution in more than 60 years.Hegseth said in an interview with conservative TV outlet Real America's Voice that Hasan is "gonna get a firing squad of soldiers. As it should be".Asked if Hasan had made any final requests or reached out to President Donald Trump, Hegseth said: "Don't care. We'll see him on December 3rd."Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell had said on Monday that the defence secretary had made the recommendation and Trump approved it.The BBC has contacted the White House for comment on whether Trump supports a livestreamed public execution.While there were more than 2,700 executions across 17 countries last year, only two countries carried them out publicly.Eleven public executions were known to have been carried out in Iran in 2025, and another six in Afghanistan, according to Amnesty International.The execution is scheduled to take place at Fort Hood in Texas on 3 December, the secretary of the US Army said on Tuesday. It will be the first military execution by firing squad since the end of World War Two.Hasan, a US Army psychiatrist from Virginia, admitted in court that he was the gunman in the deadliest ever non-combat attack on an American military base.The shooting on 5 November 2009 took place in a crowded medical building where deploying soldiers were awaiting check-ups and vaccines.At court Hasan apologised for "any mistakes". He said during his court martial in 2013 that he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan.A military execution requires approval from the US president, according to military law. It also requires appellate review, where a higher court inspects the decision, and a final judgment on its legality to move forward.The appellate process for Hasan is not over, Mills said, and he is likely to seek review of his conviction and sentence in federal court, which would likely stay the execution. As such, Mills said that he would be surprised if the execution happened."Seeking to make it livestreamed, a firing squad execution, is little more than attention-seeking by the Trump administration and is unlikely to occur, much less deliver any semblance of justice," he added.Eugene R Fidell, a visiting lecturer at Yale Law School, told the BBC it was a "really unfortunate decision"."To livestream an execution is just so out of the Middle Ages. In a way, we are so past that as a society, at least I thought so until today," he said.Fidell said if Hasan pursued legal action, the "proceedings would last years" and "far longer than President Trump's term in the White House".Certain states require some form of public viewing of executions. Many states require journalists to be present, and the person due to be executed can invite people. Others also allow ordinary citizens to volunteer as witnesses.But "there hasn't ever been a livestreamed execution," says Deborah Denno, a law professor at Fordham University, who has studied US execution methods.A livestreamed execution would "force a level of transparency that we have probably never seen before in this country", she says. "More than half of the country wants the death penalty - even though that's on the decline - an argument could be made that 'if you want the death penalty, then we are going to show you how it's conducted in this country'. And people would have to realise exactly what's happening in a way that many people ignore."Denno says there are important considerations for a livestream such as whether it would be age-restricted and whether it would contravene the policies of the online platform that hosts the viewing.It is unclear where the livestream will be available. Most major social media platforms have rules that prohibit or restrict livestreaming explicit content.Meta, YouTube, TikTok and X, the most notable and widely used online platforms capable of streaming live video, have prohibitions in place on not only violent images and videos, but those that show death.Meta, the owner of Instagram, Facebook and Threads, explicitly bans any live stream of capital punishment.TikTok has a similar blanket ban. Its policy reads, "We don't allow extremely graphic, violent, or disturbing content—especially when it could cause viewers emotional distress."The policy at X, which has loosened content moderation since Elon Musk took over the platform, says that any content depicting when a person dies will be removed "if we receive a request from their family or an authorized representative."The BBC has reached out for comment to the companies.Truth Social, the social media platform owned by Trump, does not have a live-stream video feature for users.The countries with the highest number of executions last year were China, Iran, Saudi Arabia, Yemen and the US, in that order, Amnesty International data shows.While Trump has never publicly advocated for a public execution, he has long supported the death penalty. In 1989, for example, he took out large ads in The New York Times calling for the execution of the group dubbed the Central Park Five - who had been convicted of rape and assault charges but were later exonerated.Trump has previously condemned public executions in Iran, and has cited the Iranian government's potential killing of protesters as a possible justification for military intervention before attacking the country earlier this year.The US government had not executed anyone for 17 years until the final year of Trump's first term as president, when the government conducted a flurry of 13 executions.Upon returning to office last January, Trump swiftly overturned predecessor Joe Biden's moratorium on federal executions and signed an executive order aimed at "restoring" the death penalty and "protecting public safety".The last military execution in the country took place in 1961, when a US Army private was hanged after being convicted of raping an 11-year-old Austrian girl. The execution was authorised by then-President Dwight D Eisenhower and took place despite the victim's family asking his successor, John F Kennedy, for clemency.The last military execution by firing squad took place in January 1945, when a young US Army deserter, Eddie Slovik, was shot during the final months of the World War Two.With additional reporting by Kwasi Gyamfi Asiedu and Kali Hays

schema.headline: Fort Hood attacker's execution by firing squad will be livestreamed, Pentagon says

title: Asos hackers took more personal details than first revealed, BBC finds
description: Asos has told its customers that hackers are in possession of detailed profiles of potentially millions of the online store's users.It issued the upda
body: Asos has told its customers that hackers are in possession of detailed profiles of potentially millions of the online store's users.It issued the update after BBC News told the retailer it had been contacted by cyber criminals who said this week's breach went beyond the "basic contact details" Asos previously said might have been accessed.Names, addresses, phone numbers, emails, customer numbers and dates of birth are now in the hands of criminals.One victim told the BBC it was "very unsettling" that the hackers now know these things about her.The criminals also have access to the searches customers have made on the website. Terms like "reclaimed vintage", "glamorous wide fit" and "Asos petite" are visible in the data.Harriet has been using Asos since 2019 - another detail the hackers now know. "What I find particularly worrying is the possibility that stolen data can be used as a tool for for future attacks, meaning the impact of a breach could extend well beyond the initial incident," she said.With the stolen information, scammers may be able to create convincing phishing attack emails or phone calls.The risk to individuals is now higher and customers are being warned about potential impersonation scams.In its email to customers, Asos confirmed data profiles were taken but said no bank details or passwords were accessed."Please remain cautious of unexpected messages or calls claiming to be from Asos," it said. "We will never ask you to share passwords, security codes or payment details through an unsolicited message or call."The company did not respond to questions about the scale of the breach.Asos said it is still investigating the data breach and it would "contact customers directly where we believe additional information, support or action may be required".The UK fashion site explained to customers that hackers gained access to an Asos employee account by "impersonating a trusted contact to obtain log in credentials".With that log in to an unnamed service, the hackers were able to download the customer data.In the pop up notification send to customers by the hackers, they claimed they had "compromised the Snowflake instance".Snowflake is a popular data storage and analysis company whose customers have been breached in the past due to unauthorised log ins.The cyber criminals, calling themselves Xuanyewen, claimed to the BBC they used a platform which is built natively on top of Snowflake - called Simon AI - to gain access to the data.Simon AI has been contacted for comment. Snowflake previously said its platform had not been breached. Asos said customers are not being asked to take any action. But cyber security experts have warned users to change passwords as a precaution and be on alert for suspicious activity."Passwords have not been stolen, so be highly suspicious of any unsolicited text or email asking you to change or share yours," said Trevor Dearing, Senior Director of Critical Infrastructure at Illumio."Expect scammers to mention the attack, use your personal details to seem genuine, and create urgency, such as threatening to lock your account within 24 hours."Asos said its website and app are safe to use and "we know our customers trust us with their information". "We take that responsibility seriously and have already taken additional steps to further strengthen security controls," it said.

schema.headline: Asos hackers took more personal details than first revealed, BBC finds

title: 'I don't know what my partner earns': How soon into dating should you reveal your salary?
description: Figure caption, Watch: How soon into dating do you talk about your salary? We ask New Yorkers and LondonersByYasmin RufoBusiness reporter Reporting fr
body: Figure caption, Watch: How soon into dating do you talk about your salary? We ask New Yorkers and LondonersByYasmin RufoBusiness reporter Reporting fromNew YorkUpdated 4 hours agoYou know their favourite restaurant, what happened with their ex and their most embarrassing childhood story. But do you know how much your partner earns?Money remains one of dating's trickier conversations. Bring it up too early and it can sound like you're sizing up their bank balance. But leave it too long and you could be planning a future with someone without knowing much about their finances at all.We spoke to 20-somethings in New York City to see if there was a sweet spot for when to talk salaries.Image caption, Willa says she doesn't know what her partner earns even though he knows her salary Willa Morton, 25, says she doesn't think couples necessarily need to reveal their salaries at all."It's just a number and you can gauge how much someone makes based on the way they live and how much they spend," she says.Willa, who works in tech sales, has talked to her boyfriend about not earning very much herself but hasn't asked him for a figure in return.He's a company founder and, though his income varies, she knows that he earns more than she does."He's more free-spending whereas I'm always saying, 'That's too expensive, that costs too much, we don't need to spend that.'"Their dates typically cost around $200 (£150) and he usually pays, while she picks up smaller bills such as coffees."It's an unspoken rule that he will pick up the bigger bills."Image caption, Vik says if someone brought up salary and spending on a first date they probably wouldn't be the right person for himFor many, there's a fairly clear dividing line as to when you talk about salary, spending habits and debt and that's when you become an official couple.Alexa Ludato, 25, who works in insurance, says she'd only have the conversation when she was official with someone.Before then, she would "like to have an idea of what their job is, but not how much they make".Her friend, Vik Sunderaj, 22, agrees. "You should only discuss it once you get into a serious relationship."He thinks a salary question on the first few dates is "a little crazy"."If they asked, I would be honest, but I wouldn't bring it up," he says. And if his date really wanted to know his salary, "it probably means they wouldn't be the right person for me".'Asking my salary is a red flag'Others feel even more strongly about being asked too soon. Twenty-six-year-old Bridget Shurdut, who works in sales, says she would find it "incredibly odd" if someone asked about her salary within the first few dates."I don't think I'd continue to see that person. I'd answer the question, but it would be a red flag for me."For her, someone's current salary isn't necessarily particularly useful information anyway as she says she's much more interested in "whether someone is ambitious and driven than what they earn monetarily".Dating and relationship coach Kate Mansfield, says money conversations "should start much earlier than many people think". "In the first few dates you should talk about how each of you approaches spending, saving, generosity, lifestyle and financial independence as these things shape compatibility." Image caption, Emily's been in a relationship for two years and has not discussed salaries yetBecoming official doesn't necessarily mean swapping payslips though.Insurance worker Emily Moretta, 26, has been with her boyfriend for two years and says they still haven't explicitly told each other their salaries and "he doesn't know how much I make".She assumes he probably has a rough idea, but says neither has ever felt the need to ask."Maybe down the line we would, when it gets more serious," she says, adding that they would have to be at the stage of moving in together before talking about it.

schema.headline: 'I don't know what my partner earns': How soon into dating should you reveal your salary?

title: Protesters blame 'vulture funds' for Spain's housing crisis
description: Pierina Nicuray, a 21-year-old university graduate, has spent a week camped out in Madrid's Puerta del Sol square. Like many of the hundreds of others
body: Pierina Nicuray, a 21-year-old university graduate, has spent a week camped out in Madrid's Puerta del Sol square. Like many of the hundreds of others who have pitched their tents here to protest at Spain's housing crisis, she has no doubts when it comes to diagnosing the cause."It's the same problem as always," she says. "A lack of homes."She adds: "Landlords are taking advantage of the situation to raise rentals, and then there's also Airbnb."Jorge Moreno, a 19-year-old film-dubbing student who has also been living in a tent here in central Madrid for the last few days, agrees."There are so many homes standing empty because they have been bought by vulture funds and investment funds which hike up the rent of people living in properties until they get rid of them," says Jorge, who lives with his mother and fears it will be a long time before he can afford a home of his own."They've been making a business of housing for a long time," he adds. "But it's an abusive business which stops Spaniards from being able to live in a decent home."His and Pierina's diagnoses are frequently voiced by fellow protesters, ordinary Spaniards and even the Spanish government. On presenting a recent package of emergency measures to tackle the housing problem, Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said he was legislating "against those who consider housing just another object on the market with which to speculate".Those reforms were rejected by Congress, prompting Sánchez to call a snap election next month.Nicuray and Moreno can point to the single case that sparked the current Spanish housing protest movement as proof that profit-driven practices are at the heart of the crisis: the 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal was evicted from her home after the investment firm that had bought it tried to persuade her to leave, then sharply increased her rent, which she was unable to pay.Although the social backlash that followed caused the company to invite Abascal to return to her old home, she never did, dying in hospital on Wednesday.Many others have their own stories of struggling with a soaring rental market.Carmen Pérez is a retired widow, originally from Ecuador, who has been living in Spain for 17 years. When she arrived, housing was relatively cheap and accessible, but - as costs have risen - she has been forced to move in with her daughter and son-in-law as she looks for somewhere affordable to rent."When a property is listed to rent, there's always a long waiting list," she says. "And the rent is always too high for me. All of this has affected my health - I've got depression, I don't have any stability or security."Spain has seen an average rise in rental costs of 84% over the last 10 years, according to property outlet Idealista. In the centre of the southern city of Málaga, the increase has been 113 %, and, in Marbella - just under 150%.Such numbers have made housing Spaniards' biggest concern. A recent study by the Centre for Sociological Research (CIS) showed how the broader Spanish population, like the protesters, want to see action taken against those perceived to be powerful movers in the housing market. Some 72% wanted higher taxes introduced for those with 10 or more properties; 76% wanted limits on short-term tourist accommodation; and 40% supported the expropriation of empty homes.However, Jorge Galindo, director at the Esade centre for economic policy, says that available data makes it difficult to know exactly how many Spanish properties are owned by so-called "vulture funds" and being used for speculation. He points to Bank of Spain figures from 2024 showing that only 8% of properties for rent are owned by companies.Galindo says he concludes from the data available that there is not a notable accumulation of property to rent among a small number of owners in Spain."When it comes to explaining the rise in rentals, that is not the big cause," he says. "What explains it is the shortage of supply compared to demand over recent years."The Bank of Spain appears to agree, and has estimated that the country has a housing shortfall of around 750,000 homes. The institution's deputy governor, Soledad Núñez, warned in September that by 2028 that could rise to one million.There are 3.8 million empty properties in Spain, according to the National Statistics Institute (INE), but a large number of those are in depopulated rural areas and therefore have little relevance to the current crisis, which is most acute in urban hubs. Other explanations for this high number include properties awaiting renovation, or legal disputes between family members who have inherited them.Demographic changes play a major part in the imbalance between supply and demand. Between 2021 and 2025, there were about 1.2 million new households in Spain, driven in great part by the arrival of migrants who have played a major role in the country's recent economic growth.However, house building has not kept pace, with fewer than half-a-million new homes during that period. That was partly because Spain's construction industry had shrunk in the wake of the Eurozone crisis, while the cost of materials rose substantially after Covid, and a lack of political consensus put legal obstacles in the way of building."It was not a priority for us to build new houses," Galindo says. "But, once the demographic boom came, we realised how costly it was for us."He adds that short-term tourist accommodation, like Airbnb, which has been identified by both the Spanish government and many activists as a culprit, is likely to have had a more localised effect, pushing up prices in specific urban areas rather than having an overall impact.Meanwhile, the crisis has been aggravated by lagging salaries. A study by El País found that, in real terms, the average Spaniard had 5% less spending power than a decade ago, due to taxes, social security and inflation. The average monthly salary in the Madrid region is €1,550 (£1,314; $1,738)."No worker should have to spend 75% or 80% of their salary on rent, because what are they supposed to eat?" says Francisco Pardo, an 81-year-old retired taxi driver, who sympathises with the protesters, during a visit to the tent city in Madrid. "Many workers don't even earn €2,000 [per month]."The case of Maricarmen has suddenly made the housing crisis an urgent topic of discussion, not just in Madrid's Puerta del Sol but across the country. The question now is whether a consensus can be reached on how to solve it.

schema.headline: Protesters blame 'vulture funds' for Spain's housing crisis

title: ICE agent shoots man in New York City
description: A US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent shot a man in the Bronx in New York City on Thursday.The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), w
body: A US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent shot a man in the Bronx in New York City on Thursday.The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which runs the agency, confirmed an ICE officer "discharged his weapon" during "a targeted enforcement operation... to arrest a criminal illegal alien".In a statement, it added the man was alive and at a local hospital.New York mayor Zohran Mamdani said it was an "unconscionable and incredibly serious situation"."Early reports indicate agents surrounded him and a five-year-old child in his car before firing multiple rounds. We believe the child was physically unharmed," he said.The BBC has approached DHS for comment about Mamdani's remarks.Late on Thursday evening, New York Governor Kathy Hochul said she had spoken to President Donald Trump about the shooting and had expressed "outrage on behalf of New Yorkers"."I also asked that any body camera footage of the shooting be released to the public so we can establish the facts and get to the truth."Trump has not yet commented publicly on the shooting.The DHS said the man, who has not been named by officials, was from the Dominican Republic and had "a prior criminal conviction for grand larceny, and multiple prior arrests for assault, robbery, possession of drugs, and weapons possession".It also claimed he was associated with the Trinitarios, described by the US justice department as a transnational criminal group.

schema.headline: ICE agent shoots man in New York City

title: Singapore Grand Prix: George Russell says he will take another grid penalty this season
description: "I knew I was going to have a penalty," Russell said. "The plan was always to go in Austin, and obviously Singapore is the second hardest track to ove
body: "I knew I was going to have a penalty," Russell said. "The plan was always to go in Austin, and obviously Singapore is the second hardest track to overtake on on the calendars. So you would never choose to do it (here)."But we have no engines because of all of the various failures, so there was no engine I could have reverted to from earlier in the season. With the failure I had to take it."We don't have the (upgrade) this weekend, and because there are seven races remaining, you can either choose to roll the dice and hope it lasts for seven races, but also suffer a performance offset (as the engine degrades), or just accept I'll be taking another penalty."Antonelli will also likely have another back-of-the-grid penalty when the upgraded engine is introduced, following his previous one at the Italian Grand Prix, which he won from 19th on the grid.Russell will also be reverting to an older specification car in Singapore this weekend.Mercedes introduced an aerodynamic upgrade in Malaysia last weekend, but it did not give the car the performance uplift expected.So in an attempt to prove whether that was because of idiosyncrasies to do with the Sepang track or a problem with the upgrade itself, Mercedes is splitting the specification of their cars.Russell will drive the specification with which he won in Azerbaijan, the week before Malaysia, while Antonelli will run the new spec.Russell said: "I actually asked a question already on Friday in Sepang. At the end of the day it's the car I'm reverting to is a car that was on pole by 0.8secs and Kimi won the race before, so it's important to remember the context. It's not like reverting back to a launch car."Given the circumstances of the grid penalty as well, it just seemed like a no-brainer. For me, unfortunately we're not going to be fighting for a podium this weekend, it's exceptionally unlikely, so it's more important for us to try and understand, was Malaysia a one-off or was it the upgrade?"Russell's retirement in Malaysia, along with Antonelli finishing second to Red Bull's Max Verstappen, meant the Italian's lead in the drivers' championship has extended to 84 points.Both Mercedes drivers have suffered reliability problems this year but Russell believes his season has been disproportionately affected by factors outside his control."I've probably had more failures this year than I've had in the three seasons put together, and of course it's tough to take," he said."If I'm being 100% fair with myself, as I've said before, the performance this season hasn't been strong enough, and it probably would have affected me more if I'd have still been in the fight."But obviously the pressure and the momentum, every setback has an impact on that momentum."Since the start of the year (an engine failure) in Canada was the big one, and then, you know, the drive-through penalty in Monaco. The loss at the weekend has basically compromised two weekends for me."Two races, Silverstone and Spa, with the PU issues we had (involving a loss of performance from the engine), it's been pretty incredible how things have panned out this year, but I think just focus on what you can control."

schema.headline: Singapore Grand Prix: George Russell says he will take another grid penalty this season

title: Celebrity Traitors episode three: Emotions run high as two players banished
description: Emotions run high at the round table as Celebrity Traitors banish two playersImage caption, Actress Sharon Rooney was visibly shocked to find which pl
body: Emotions run high at the round table as Celebrity Traitors banish two playersImage caption, Actress Sharon Rooney was visibly shocked to find which players returned to breakfast during Thursday's episodeBySteven McIntoshEntertainment reporterSpoiler warning: This article reveals details from the third episode of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.We normally expect raised voices, conflicting theories and a dramatic showdown from the Celebrity Traitors. But as this year's first round table got under way, the writing was on the castle wall.Viewers who often get frustrated with the faithful and root for them to uncover a traitor had their wish firmly Richard E Grant-ed on Thursday, as the actor was banished in a landslide vote.His questionable strategy of revealing he was a traitor to the other celebrities in the bar led to the first time in the UK version of the show that a traitor has been identified at the opening round table."Thank you for giving me an almost bingo full-house of votes," Grant told his fellow players. "I have always wanted to be a traitor, and sometimes in life your dreams do come true."There was jubilation from the other celebrities as Grant confirmed his identity, waving his hands in the air. Ross Kemp was so happy it came out as borderline anger, with a vein-popping "get in there!"Other players seemed genuinely shocked. "This is me with men all the time," joked comedian Joanne McNally, who hadn't voted for Grant. "I completely believed him!"But although the faithful had successfully found a traitor, and even managed to spell his name correctly on their slates, the first round table saw some other players behave in ways that immediately aroused suspicion.Image caption, Myha'la winked at Richard E Grant before voting for him - which was picked up by some other playersImage caption, Ross Kemp, meanwhile, was a scary level of delighted to have rumbled GrantJulie Hesmondhalgh noticed Myha'la ostentatiously winking at Grant before she voted for him, which later prompted the former Coronation Street actress to make one of the most impassioned - but mistaken - speeches of the night."It was traitor-on-traitor," she declared (it wasn't). "I don't know if anybody else saw it," (we did). "I am so excited because I truly believe we can get two in a row," (don't count on it).Where is the Traitors castle, and can you visit it?Traitors commit first murder as Grant tries to save his skinCelebrity Traitors cast: Who are this year's 'big dogs' and dark horses?The remaining traitors, Maya Jama and James Acaster, met in the turret later with the choice of murdering previously shortlisted players Jerry Hall and Hannah Fry, or seducing a third traitor to replace Grant.The pair ultimately decided to recruit mathematician Fry, who had the most wonderful and meme-able reaction when she found out that, not only was she not being murdered, she was being seduced.Accepting the offer, Fry joined Jama and Acaster in the turret, exclaiming as she learned their identities: "I had both of you down as faithful!"The new trio discussed how they would approach breakfast the next morning, before Acaster delivered the line of the episode."It's changing a lot, this Traitors," he observed of the fluid line-up. "It's like the Sugababes."Image caption, "I managed to checkmate myself," said Grant, "which as far as I'm aware, has never been done"Image caption, Mathematician Hannah Fry was shocked to find she was being recruited instead of murderedThe next morning, there were shocked faces when the players realised everybody had made it to breakfast unscathed, with the celebrities concluding that one player must have been recruited."It was fascinating seeing Jerry and Hannah come back," said Miranda Hart. "Hannah seemed different, as if something new has happened to her." Oh yes? "I definitely clocked a nervousness in her, which is very interesting."We could have a first-rate traitor hunter on our hands here. But would any of Hart's fellow players feel the same way? "Poor Hannah," said McNally, "she's been recruited." Uh-oh.As the theories continued to float around across various sub-meetings, with Hesmondhalgh, Bella Ramsey and several others setting their sights on Myha'la, the celebrities headed out to the next mission. Presenter Claudia Winkleman explained the latest task would see them use a battering ram to break down the doors of four crypts, where they could find money to add to the prize pot - and also potentially bag some shields.James Blunt immediately took control, assigning players various roles. "He was full army officer," Hart observed. "I found it mildly erotic.""I don't think I've ever used a battering ram," Joe Lycett reflected. "I would use a battering ram to get into [Wicked star] Jonathan Bailey's house, but that's it."Image caption, Miranda Hart joked that she found James Blunt's command of the latest task "mildly erotic"Myha'la and Fry entered one crypt, found a shield and debated who should keep it. They agreed on Myha'la, partly because she had grabbed it first, although she sweetly suggested that the pair could keep it secret from the other players to protect both of them.Jama and Sharon Rooney, meanwhile, scored two further shields, but the players then found that some shields would have to be given up anyway in order to unlock the final chest of prize money.Rooney and Myha'la surrendered theirs, but traitor Jama quietly held on to hers. The other players didn't know she had one, and the TV presenter asked Rooney to keep it secret. That decision could come back to bite her in later episodes.In the cars on the way back, the players continued to debate various hunches, with one particularly awkward journey where Myha'la and Hesmondhalgh admitted they were suspicious of each other."I feel like you've been a little bit vague," said Hesmondhalgh. "That's only because I've thought it's been you from day one," Myha'la replied.We've certainly come a long way from the pair's first exchange just two episodes ago. "It's lovely to meet you Myha'la, I'm such a big fan!" - "Oh my God, thank you!"Back in the castle, Rob Beckett had adopted a new policy. "When someone comes up to talk to me, I just agree with them, whatever they say," he laughed in the castle's diary room.Image caption, James Acaster joked that he wanted to murder James Blunt to avoid confusion over them sharing a nameAs the players gathered for the second banishment of the episode, discussion inevitably turned to prime suspect Myha'la."I've heard my name a whole bunch today," she acknowledged, as the others struggled to square her behaviour during the mission.The actress became visibly emotional as she recounted the events of the crypt and attempted to justify grabbing the shield before offering it to Fry. "I was going to give it to her," Myha'la said tearfully. "I was worried about my protection, but I thought maybe [Fry] had more heat."Sensing that the tide was turning against Myha'la, Fry stuck the knife in. "Why would you scrabble for the shield, and then be keen to give it away?" she asked.Watch on iPlayer with new episodes every Thursday and Friday The latest banished and murdered celebs have their say in UncloakedDespite a sprinkling of votes for other players, Myha'la became the second casualty of the episode. "I have loved getting to know you all," she said as she confirmed her faithful status to the other players. Hart became even more suspicious of Fry, however, after realising the mathematician had orchestrated events to make Myha'la's behaviour at the crypt look less innocent. "Miss Marple is so on," Hart said with a smile.Later, the traitors met in the turret and debated who their next victim should be, settling on a shortlist of Blunt, Ramsey and Sebastian Croft.Acaster had a characteristically unique reason for suggesting James Blunt. "It would make my life easier," he said, "because every time someone says 'James', I'm turning around, and half the time, it's for him."Celebrity Traitors continues on Friday at 20:00 BST on BBC One and iPlayer.

schema.headline: Celebrity Traitors episode three: Emotions run high as two players banished

title: Man City charges: Enzo Maresca says 'feeling is fantastic' among Man City squad
description: Manchester City head coach Enzo Maresca says the "feeling is fantastic" among his players and they "don't care too much about the noise" surrounding t
body: Manchester City head coach Enzo Maresca says the "feeling is fantastic" among his players and they "don't care too much about the noise" surrounding the club after it was found guilty of the majority of the 115 charges brought against it by the Premier League.The club's international players returned to training on Thursday, nine days after the Premier League published a damning report that stated the club had used "sham" contracts to disguise secret funding of more than £830m.BBC Sport reported this week that Maresca would address the players upon their return to domestic duty after news of the verdict broke while the majority of the squad were away with their respective nations.It is understood the City head coach asked his players not to allow the crisis that has engulfed the club to affect their attitude and focus as the Premier League campaign gets back under way this weekend."The feeling is fantastic, to be honest," Maresca said in an in-house interview when asked about the mood among his squad prior to their trip to face Liverpool on Sunday (16:30 BST)."The players are excited for the next two games. But especially they are excited because in this moment we are top of the league. The players are just focused on that. "They know what we can control is the football side - they are not worried at all about different things. "They know their profession and they know that the noise is there, but they don't care too much about the noise. They are just focused in this moment on how we can beat Liverpool and how, together with the fans, we can try to win in Anfield."Maresca added he felt "calm" and his squad trusts the club "completely".City have launched an appeal and have publicly maintained their innocence.The private communication to those with links to the playing staff at City has been equally as emphatic, it is understood.Speaking to Sky Sports, striker Erling Haaland echoed his manager's sentiments, saying: "I care a lot about this place. I spent my first four years here, it's a special place for us. I care a lot about City and the fans. I am a fan myself. I feel with them."The fans will have a good time on Sunday - we have to stick together. We have to stay with each other and stay positive. No matter what happens in life, we always have to smile. Stay positive, look ahead, and try to win football games and enjoy the situation."We have to stick together and spread the love to each other. Enjoy the ride and smile."As Premier League football returns following a three-week hiatus, managers of rival clubs can expect to be asked to comment on the City verdict during their compulsory pre-match press conferences. Nottingham Forest boss Oliver Glasner will face the media on Friday but told reporters earlier in the week he hopes the process is completed "as soon as possible". Glasner joined Forest from Crystal Palace in the summer and cited his experience of the latter's demotion from the Europa League to the Conference League in 2025 after the club breached multi-club ownership rules."Let's wait until the final verdict is spoken, but my wish is just that this is quick," Glasner said."Because we didn't know with Palace if we were in the Europa League or Conference League and then it was 'you will hear on Thursday' and then that became Monday, because it was always delayed. Then we got the final verdict 10 days before the Conference League started."That's why I think this must be [completed] as soon as possible. "There is still damage for the Premier League, not just in England. It's a big topic all over the world, especially in Europe. "The most important thing is the integrity of the league because as soon as the fans can't trust it, they won't watch it any more."Some manager news conferences were held on Thursday and Leeds head coach Daniel Farke and Newcastle's Matthias Jaissle both steered clear of commenting at length on the matter.It is understood a number of clubs have already taken a clear stance for their managers not to comment.Coventry boss Frank Lampard - who played for City in the 2014-15 season - said the players will not feel they have lost their titles even if the club is stripped of them because it is part of their personal history.City have yet to be punished but BBC Sport has been told there has been little appetite from within the Premier League - both the organisation and its clubs - for past titles to be taken from them. "I have titles and I don't have my titles hanging on my wall at home, I have them in my head," said Lampard, who won the Premier League three times with Chelsea."You are competing against the best in the Premier League and a lot of things are out of [your] control but you are competing against the best and they're very hard to win."So I think it would be very hard to take someone's title away as a player individually as they should be in your head as opposed to in a beautiful glass cabinet or whatever. I know there are some who do that."Lampard made 38 appearances and scored eight goals when he joined City in 2014 after 13 years at Chelsea.
